newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak central banker reaffirms tight money policy.
newsitem.headline: Slovak central banker reaffirms tight money policy.

text.p: Slovak central bank (NBS) Governor Vladimir Masar on Wednesday reaffirmed the NBS' tight monetary policy, saying it would be revised only if the government's expansive spending plan is moderated.
"We are not stepping aside from our monetary goals," Masar told a news conference.
Referring to the approved state budget that forecasts the deficit to widen to 36.9 billion crowns from a 25.5 billion crown shortfall in 1996, Masar said:

"Once we have a guaranteed certainty that some of the government-supported projects will be backed off from, or that the expansion (of the budget deficit) will be less significant, we of course could correct (loosen) our policy."

Masar's statement comes just weeks after the government criticised the NBS's restrictive money policy. The government subsequently appointed former deputy finance minister Jozef Magula to the NBS's governing board.

The NBS tightened its policy several times last year, culminating in a series of steps late in 1996 after the government approved a 1997 fiscal deficit of 3.7 percent of GDP, after a 0.4 percent surplus in 1996.
Local bankers have been watching for signs that the government may reduce NBS independence and force it to loosen its monetary policy.

Masar added that though state budget financing has been developing "favourably" in the first two months of the year, which in turn has had "favourable" monetary effects, the NBS is prepared for it to worsen.

"Concluding on the expectation of the state budget deficit development continuing unfavourably in the coming months, we are prepared to react even if the approved budget plans are followed," Masar said.
"We have the instruments for it," Masar added. He did not elaborate.

Masar also said that he expected banks to raise interest rates on loans by one or two percentage points based on the preliminary figures for January and planned interest rates for March. The average credit rate in December was 13.45 percent.
While interbank rates have risen from end 1996 levels, few banks have increased credit prices for its corporate and retail clients, Masar said.
